titulo: robos-impressos — print, assemble, and connect your pet robot at home
meta: Four robots to 3D print: a dinosaur, a capybara, a square desktop robot, and a square robot on wheels. Files are already oriented for printing, with a shopping list and estimated prices, step-by-step assembly, and wire-by-wire connections. Parts are generated with code and checked by a script.

hero_chip: Robots to print at home · [[VERSAO]] · project not yet printed
hero_h1: Make your pet robot your own, printed by you
hero_lead: You want a robot that looks like an animal, made by you, and you don’t want to find out halfway through that a part doesn’t fit or that no one told you what to buy. On robos-impressos, you choose one of four robots, print the parts, assemble and wire it, following the shopping list and the wire-by-wire wiring diagram. Each part goes through a program that checks the fit before you spend any filament.
hero_alt: Render of the project's four robots on a wooden table: a green dinosaur, an orange capybara with a green bandana, a square desktop robot, and a square robot with wheels, with the title Your printed robot
hero_cap: Render made from the project's 3D models, the same ones used to generate the print files. This is not a photo: nothing has been printed yet.
resumo: You want to build a friendly robot at home and don’t know where to start: which parts to print, what to buy, where each wire goes. robos-impressos is a set of four robots to 3D print: a dinosaur and a [[DINO_ALTURA]] cm capybara that move across the floor; a [[CUBO_ALTURA]] cm square desktop robot with a screen for a face; and a [[RODAS_ALTURA]] cm square robot on wheels. Each has its own page, with files already positioned for printing, a shopping list with estimated prices and links, a print guide, and a wire-by-wire wiring diagram. It’s for anyone with access to a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate who wants to build, learn, or teach robotics. It isn’t a cheap project: purchased parts alone cost between R$ [[CUSTO_MIN]] and R$ [[CUSTO_MAX]], depending on the robot, not including filament or tools. This is phase 1: the printed body, assembled and wired. The program (movement, voice, camera, intelligence) is phase 2 and hasn’t been made yet. And an honest note: this is a digital project checked by script. No one has printed these parts yet, and the electrical setup has not been bench-tested.
grade_alt: Render of the four robots on the table and six steps: choose a model, print the parts, fit the servos, assemble the shell, swiveling head, ready for phase 2
nota_banner: The two banners and the robot images are renders: computer-generated images made from the project files, not photos of an assembled robot.
modelos_sub: Each robot has its own page with everything you need: shopping list, files, printing, assembly, and connections.

dino_txt: Moves on two wheels hidden in its thighs, with a support ball at the back. Turns and tilts its head, opens its mouth, and moves both arms.

capi_txt: Sitting, with a green bandana. Moves on two wheels hidden in its hips and two support balls at the front, under its paws. Turns and tilts its head and opens its mouth.

cubo_txt: For a desk; it doesn't move on wheels. Its head is a cube with a 3.5-inch screen for a face: it turns almost a full rotation and tilts up and down.

rodas_txt: The same cube head, with a 5-inch screen, on a base with two 85 mm wheels and motors with encoders. It turns and tilts its head and moves across the floor.
rodas_nivel: Advanced: [[R_PECAS]] parts, [[R_SERVOS]] servos, and 2 motors with encoders
rodas_link: Open the robot on wheels page

modelos_mont: Assembly time is estimated by counting tasks, from workbench prep to the closed robot: [[M_BANCADA]] min per workbench task, [[M_PASSO]] min per assembly step, [[M_FIO]] min per wire, and [[M_INSERTO]] min per insert, with a margin of [[M_FOLGA_MENOS]]% less and [[M_FOLGA_MAIS]]% more. Nothing has been assembled yet. The simplest is the robot with the fewest parts and servos, with no wheels or motors; the other three require more soldering, more wires, and more adjustments.
modelos_nota: Filament and printing time are volume-based estimates, without a slicer. Prices are in Brazilian reais, shown as ranges: "phase 1 parts" does not include filament or tools; "from scratch" adds the parts, 2 rolls of filament, and all tools. Each robot's page says where each price came from.
como_h2: Inside: a skeleton with the shell on top
como_sub: The PETG skeleton bears the weight. The PLA shell just covers the robot and comes off without taking the skeleton apart.
esq_alt: Render of the dinosaur without its shell: the dark chassis with the wheels, motors, board trays, and neck parts
como1_p: The parts that bear loads are made of PETG: the chassis, which holds the motors, battery, and boards, and the neck parts. The screws and brass threaded inserts go into these parts.
exp_alt: Render of the capybara exploded view: head with eyes and jaw, bandana collar, body, rear door with the tail, and chassis with the boards, motors, and battery
como2_t: The shell in a few large parts
como2_p: On the animal robots, the shell consists of three large parts (body, rear cover, and collar) plus the head. Each prints upright, like a vase, with almost no support. No screws are visible from the front.
capiv_alt: Render of the assembled capybara, in four views
como3_p: On the animal robots, the head rotates and tilts around a sphere hidden in the collar. This lets it move side to side and up and down without opening a gap.
cuboexp_alt: Render of the square desktop robot exploded view: head shell, frame with the Raspberry Pi and screen, face panel, fork, neck with gears, cover, and base with the boards
como4_t: The square one turns almost a full rotation
como4_p: A standard servo only turns halfway around. In both square robots, two printed gears double that rotation, and the cables run up inside the neck, which is a hollow tube.
mv_nota: These are the mechanical limits, checked to make sure no parts collide. The servos and program provide the actual movement; that’s phase 2.
comum_sub: What you learn by building one applies to the others.
c1_p: Raspberry Pi, Arduino Uno with Sensor Shield, MG996R servos, 18650 batteries with a protection board and USB-C charging. The three robots on wheels also have a motor driver.
c2_p: Every part fits on a 256 mm build plate, has walls at least 2 mm thick, and prints without supports whenever possible. Where supports are unavoidable, they go inside or underneath.
c3_p: A small test coupon, identical for all four, checks the threaded insert and screw holes on your printer before the first large part.
c4_p: All measurements are kept in a single file. The same generator designs the parts for all four, and the same checker verifies them.
c5_t: Parts shared by both animal robots
c5_p: The neck fork, the cradle that tilts the head, and the support sphere cover are the same files for the dinosaur and the capybara. The skeleton is different: each animal has its own.
c6_t: The same head and neck for both square robots
c6_p: Both square robots use the same solution: the head tilts inside and rotates using gears, on a hollow tube reinforced by 3 steel tie rods.
prova_sub: A script (a small program) opens the print files, assembles each robot on the computer, and looks for problems. There are [[N_TESTES]] tests per robot, and all four pass every test.
num1: parts to print for all four robots, all fully enclosed and intact in the file
num2: parts intersecting one another, across all tested positions
num3: is the thinnest wall measured on the animals’ shells (the target was at least 2 mm)
num4: is the largest part; the printer's build plate is 256 mm
barra_titulo: Estimated printing hours per robot (without a slicer: order of magnitude)
testes_t: The [[N_TESTES]] tests and the result for each robot
tst_1_p: The number of parts is as expected.
tst_2_p: Each file is a single, closed solid.
tst_3_p: Each part fits within 256 × 256 × 256 mm in the printing position.
tst_4_p: The shells have walls that are 2 mm or thicker.
tst_5_p: No part takes up the space of another part or component (servo, motor, board, battery), with the head, mouth, and arms at their extremes.
tst_6_p: The test itself is tested: one part is deliberately put out of place, and test 5 must flag it.
tst_7_p: Every assembled part touches another: none are floating.
tst_8_p: The center of gravity falls within the supports, with a margin of 10 mm or more, in every position.
tst_9_p: Each part enters and exits through the side indicated in the assembly, without hitting anything already assembled.
tst_10_p: A part declared support-free has no unsupported area above the limit.
tst_11_p: One part is deliberately turned upside down, and test 10 must flag it.
prova_ok_li:
• The files you download are the same ones the script checked.
  • The parts fit on the build plate, fit into place in assembly order, and do not intersect.
  • The assembled robot does not tip over with the head at any extreme.
  • Each part indicates whether it needs supports, and each robot’s overhang map shows where.
prova_nao_t: What only printing and the workbench can tell you
prova_nao_li:
• No one has printed or assembled these parts yet.
  • The electrical setup came from the component datasheets and has not been bench-tested.
  • Time and filament are volume-based estimates, without a slicer.
  • Some component measurements have no official source. They are marked NC in the shopping lists: measure your part with calipers before printing the part that touches it.
  • The tests do not measure the actual clearance on your printer, the strength of the parts in use, or the path of the tool and wires.
evo_h2: The robots look more like the drawings
evo_sub: In the previous version, the capybara and the dinosaur looked far from the reference drawing, and the guide banner was an illustration that didn't show the project robots. In this version, the animals' shapes come from a 3D mesh generated from the drawing itself, the square desktop robot was redesigned, and the banner is a render of the models. Similarity is measured by the outline on a scale from 0 to 1 (IoU).
evo_ler: How to read the number: 1 means an identical outline. It only sees the silhouette, not the color or details. Based on the examples on this page, at around 0.85 and above, the silhouette already looks like the drawing.

plano_h2: From file to assembled, powered-on robot
plano_sub: Five steps, no programming required. At the end, you have the body assembled, with servos, motors, and wires in place; making it move on its own is phase 2.
pl1_p: The square desktop robot is the simplest: [[CUBO_PECAS]] parts and no wheels. The dinosaur has [[DINO_PECAS]] parts, and the capybara has [[CAPI_PECAS]]. The square robot on wheels has [[RODAS_PECAS]] parts and is the largest of the four.
pl2_t: Read the risks and buy the parts
pl2_p: Each robot’s shopping list starts with the risks: what has not been tested yet. Each item says how many the robot uses, what it does, and the price range; click the item name to search for it.
pl3_p: It’s a small test coupon that checks the insert and screw holes on your printer. Less than an hour to print, and it can save you from reprinting a part that takes many hours.
pl4_t: Print the build plates in the suggested order
pl4_p: The files already have the parts in the right position and separated by color. The skeleton is printed in PETG, which is more durable; the shell is printed in PLA.
pl5_p: Before closing any part, solder the power wires, adjust the voltages with a multimeter, and center the servos with a ready-made program. Then seat the inserts and assemble in the order the verifier tested.
plano_nota: The complete step-by-step instructions, with every screw and wire, are on each robot’s page:
pal_h2: If any of these names are new to you
pal_dl:
Servo
A small motor that turns to an angle and stops there. It turns the head and opens the mouth.
Arduino and Raspberry Pi
Two electronic boards. The Arduino controls motors and servos; the Raspberry Pi is a small computer that handles voice and camera in phase 2.
Script
A small program. Here, it generates the parts and checks that they are correct.
Render
An image made on a computer from the 3D file. It is not a photo.
PLA and PETG
Two printing plastics. PLA gives a nice finish; PETG handles more force and heat.
Build plate
The printer’s base. “12 build plates” means 12 prints, one after another.
Support and overhang
An overhang is the part that would hang in the air during printing. Support is extra plastic the printer puts underneath it, which you remove afterward.
M3 threaded insert
A threaded brass bushing that is pressed into the plastic while hot so the 3 mm screw holds firmly.
Test coupon
A small part printed first to check the holes on your printer.
18650 battery
A rechargeable lithium battery, a little larger than a regular battery.
Motor driver
A small board that lets the Arduino turn the wheel motors on and reverse them.
Encoder
A sensor that counts the motor’s rotations so the robot knows how far it has moved.
Sensor Shield
A board that plugs on top of the Arduino to make wiring the servos easier.
Chassis, fork, and cradle
Skeleton parts: the chassis is the base that carries the motors and boards; the fork and cradle hold and tilt the head.
IoU
A measure from 0 to 1 of how much two outlines overlap. Here, the robot’s outline and the reference drawing’s outline.
NC
Not confirmed: a component measurement with no official source, which you check on your own part.
tec_h2: The kit: for anyone who wants to print, change measurements, or create another robot
tec_sub: You don't need this section to understand what you've read above.
oque_h2: Parts generated from code, not drawn by hand
oque_sub: Everything comes from a file of measurements. If you change the servo or your printer’s clearance, change one number and generate it again.
p1_p: comum/cad/parametros.py stores clearances, measurements for each component (with the source next to it), and the shape of each robot.
p2_p: comum/cad/verificar.py reads the exported STL files and rejects open parts, parts that are too large, thin walls, parts that intersect, parts that cannot fit into place, robots that tip over, and parts that would need support without warning you.
p3_p: Each robot lives in its own folder inside projetos/, with the model, STL files, build plates, documents, and zip file. Shared files go in comum/.
fluxo_sub: For the animal robots, the skin comes from a 3D mesh generated from the reference drawing; holes, pockets, and cuts are exact operations applied on top of it.
fx1_p: Creates STL and 3MF files for each part, already oriented for printing, the complete assembly (montagem.glb), and the build plate layouts.
fx2_p: Assembles the robot from the files, moves the joints to their limits, measures overlaps by shared volume, rebuilds the assembly part by part, and measures the unsupported area of each part.
fx3_p: Blender produces the images in this guide: assembled robot, four views, exploded view, skeleton, build plates, and overhang maps.
pre_sub: You don't need to install anything to print and assemble. Python and Blender are only for those who will modify the project.
pre1_p: Printer with a 256 mm build plate (the project was sized for the Bambu Lab A1; the largest part is [[N_MAIOR]] mm), PLA and PETG filament, a slicer such as Bambu Studio, and the components in the robot's shopping list.
pre2_p: Soldering iron, multimeter, small screwdrivers, and calipers. The full tool list, with estimated prices, is at the end of each robot's shopping list.
pre3_p: Python 3.12 or newer and git, to generate the parts again. Blender 4, only to recreate the images.
pre3_c: check if you already have it
guia_sub: The first two steps are the same for all four robots. The third takes you to your robot’s page. The fourth is only for those who want to change dimensions.
g1_p: Each robot has a zip with the STL files, the 3MF build plates, the Arduino program, and the guides. If you only want to print, download the zip, extract it, and open the files in your slicer: you don't need a terminal or Python.
g1_git: If you plan to change dimensions and generate the parts again, you can clone the entire repository in a terminal:
g2_p: The coupon is the same file for all four robots and is included in each zip. The drawing below shows each hole from above. Next to the micro servo window are three threaded insert holes (3,9, 4,0, and 4,1 mm) and, at the tip, the yellow motor shaft hole. The other row has four screw holes: M3 with a clearance fit, M3 that cuts a thread into the plastic (M3* in the drawing), M2,5, and M2. The project uses the 4,0 mm hole, the middle one, marked with a small dimple (● in the drawing). The M3 threaded insert must fit snugly and sit flush with the surface. None of the three pin sockets shown in the drawing are used by any of the four robots. For the square robots, only the threaded insert and M3 screw holes matter: each robot's page tells you what to test on it. If the neighboring hole works better, adjust the clearance in comum/cad/parametros.py, in the FOLGA block, and generate the parts again in step 4.

g3_t: Buy, print, assemble, and wire using your robot's page
g3_p: From here on, each robot has its own path: shopping list with cautions, build plate order, settings for each part, workbench prep steps, step-by-step assembly, and wire-by-wire connections. The two tables at the end of this section take you straight to each part.
g4_t: Generate and check (only if you changed any dimensions)
g4_p: The first command recreates all the parts; the second runs the [[N_TESTES]] tests and exits with an error if any fail.
g4_win: These commands are for Linux and macOS. On Windows, use python instead of python3, dir instead of ls, .venv\Scripts\pip instead of .venv/bin/pip, and .venv\Scripts\python instead of .venv/bin/python.

f2_h2: There is already a place for everything
f2_sub: Phase 2 (listening, speaking, seeing, walking without bumping into things, knowing where it is) has not been built. The mechanical design already has space, holes, and cable routing.
f2a_t: On the animals, the sensors are in the eyes
f2a_p: The pupil is a separate part with a pocket behind it: a camera on one side, a distance sensor on the other. On the square robots, the camera sits above the screen.
f2b_t: No technical holes on the front
f2b_p: Microphones in the nostrils or under the head, a speaker with no visible grille, sensors behind details the robot already has. Screws only underneath, behind, or inside.
f2c_t: The two boards communicate over 3 wires
f2c_p: A serial connection links the Raspberry Pi and the Arduino in all four robots. The Arduino controls servos and motors; the Raspberry Pi handles voice, camera, and decisions.
f2_nota: What already has a place in each robot, and what to buy for phase 2, is on its page:

rm2_p: Print the test coupon, measure the actual components, correct the dimensions without a power supply, assemble the first robot, and test the electrical system on the workbench.
rm3_p: Servo and motor programming, voice control, camera, sensors, and navigation around the house.
